idiom_name: ActiveRecord::Relation chaining (where/order/limit, lazy) plus Object#tap for side steps
implementation_notes: Plain Ruby chains trivially (a method returns self, or a new object), but the realization Ruby code actually uses is the framework-provided relation: `Book.where(out_of_print: false).order(:title).limit(10)` builds an ActiveRecord::Relation, every clause method returns a new relation, and the SQL runs only when the relation is enumerated (to_a/each/load), which is why a chain can be extended in a scope and consumed later. Object#tap (stdlib) yields the receiver and returns it unchanged, which adds a side step (logging, collecting ids) without breaking the chain. The other idiomatic fluid API in Ruby is the block DSL - instance_eval-evaluated configuration as in RSpec or FactoryBot - which replaces chaining with nested blocks when the 'sentence' has structure rather than a flat sequence. Choose the relation chain for queries, tap for side effects, and a plain keyword-argument constructor for configuration.
code_sketch:
scope = Book.where(out_of_print: false).order(:title).limit(10)  # lazy relation, still chainable
scope = scope.where("price < ?", 20)                             # still no query executed
books = scope.to_a                                               # enumeration runs the SQL once

def with_audit(rel) = rel.tap { |r| log.debug { "relation: #{r.to_sql}" } }
pitfalls: A relation is lazy, so `scope.count` runs a COUNT and `scope.map` loads rows: a chain that looks like it is still being assembled may already have hit the database, and a loaded relation stops accepting some further clauses usefully.

Bang methods (where!, order!, limit!) mutate the relation in place while their plain counterparts return a new one; mixing them makes the final result depend on evaluation order and on whether the relation was already loaded.

Scopes and dynamic finders resolve through method_missing on the model, so a typo raises NoMethodError only when the chain reaches that link, and a model default_scope silently prefixes every chain in the application.
